subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Hard vs. Soft Water
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Hard vs. Soft Water.

hook.text: London's hard water and Seattle's soft water produce completely different coffee from the same beans.

buildup.text: Hard water has high calcium and magnesium. It extracts well but can build limescale in equipment.

discovery.text: Soft water has few minerals. It under-extracts, producing flat, lifeless coffee.

twist.text: Chlorine in tap water creates off-flavors. A simple carbon filter removes chlorine without stripping minerals.

climax.text: Cafés in different cities taste different partly because their water is different. Location shapes flavor.

punchline.text: Same recipe, different city, different cup. Water decides.

quiz.question: What problem does very soft water cause in coffee brewing?

details.summary: Hard water, rich in calcium and magnesium, can over-extract and create chalky flavors in coffee. Soft water lacks the minerals needed for proper extraction, producing thin, sour cups. The ideal brewing water falls in a moderate range around 75 to 150 ppm hardness.
details.whyItMatters: Water hardness varies wildly by location and directly affects every cup. It is often the hidden variable when coffee tastes wrong despite correct technique.
takeaways: Hard water can cause chalky, over-extracted flavors
Soft water produces thin, under-extracted coffee
Moderate hardness around 75 to 150 ppm is ideal

faq.question: How do I know if my water is hard or soft?
faq.answer: Inexpensive TDS meters and water test strips are available online. Your local water utility also publishes annual reports. If you see white scale buildup in your kettle, your water is hard. If soap lathers easily, it is likely soft.

faq.question: Can hard water damage coffee equipment?
faq.answer: Yes. Calcium carbonate deposits, known as limescale, clog pipes, block valves, and reduce heating efficiency in espresso machines and kettles. Regular descaling with citric acid or manufacturer-recommended solutions is essential for hard-water areas.
